A +9.9pp gap on the Curaçao side. Curaçao v Côte d'Ivoire in FIFA World Cup 2026 is the match. The model has Curaçao stronger than the market does — that's the reason this fires as a Pick rather than a Pass.

On Elo, Côte d'Ivoire comes in 240 points ahead — Curaçao at 1480, Côte d'Ivoire at 1720. Both Elo numbers are pulled live from the public Elo source. No host, home-ground, or altitude adjustments apply here; the prior reads straight from Elo.

Three-way split from the model: Curaçao to win at 17%, the draw at 16%, and Côte d'Ivoire to win at 67%. The home side reads 17% on this distribution — the model's central case for Curaçao.

On the same three-way, Kalshi: Curaçao to win at 7%, the draw at 17%, and Côte d'Ivoire to win at 72%. On the Curaçao side specifically the market reads 7%, which prices out at American odds of +1329. Compared against the model's 17%, that's the +9.9pp gap the Pick rests on.

The +3pp Pick threshold isn't on the point estimate, it's on the 5th-percentile from a 100-sample bootstrap of the Elo prior plus bonuses. On Curaçao, that haircut lands the model at 13%; the market is at 7%. Even on the conservative reading, the gap is +5.8pp. The Desk's posture is that calibration sits with the closing market across recent fixtures — we're not claiming the market is generally wrong, only that this side, on this fixture, looks mispriced. Selection is the dimension this verdict adds value on.

News will move the prior. With kickoff roughly 35 days out, the model is on the weekly refresh cadence; we'll move to daily once we cross the T-5d window. On a Pick this wide, it would take material news — a missing star, a tournament dropout, a venue change — to collapse the gap below the +3pp threshold; on the narrower side of the field, a single refresh can flip Pick to Pass. Either way, the Desk re-publishes after each refresh and does not recommend a trade.
